title: LiveLoRA: Exact KV Cache Migration Across LoRA Updates for LLM Agents
summary: LiveLoRA replaces full-history re-prefill when updating a LoRA adapter for active sessions by migrating the final-block KV cache exactly, exploiting frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V down-projections so that adapter, cache, and logits are committed together. It costs approximately 4.8% decoding overhead, imposes structural constraints on the model (frozen lower blocks and fixed K/V adapter projections across versions), and adds runtime complexity for candidate K/V reconstruction and reevaluation of the latest token. It can fail if the model or adapter setup violates these assumptions, if exact-arithmetic equivalence is broken by numerical or implementation divergence, or if the validated regime (a 3B model, 32 sessions, 8K-token histories) does not match the reader's production scale or model family.
rationale: The method directly addresses adapter-version rollover for long-lived agent sessions on a single GPU, but its architectural constraints and limited validation mean the gain must be verified on the reader's own model and serving stack before adoption.
technique: Exact KV cache migration across LoRA updates

It costs approximately 4.8% decoding overhead, imposes structural constraints on the model (frozen lower blocks and fixed K/V adapter projections across versions), and adds runtime complexity for candidate K/V reconstruction and reevaluation of the latest token. It can fail if the model or adapter setup violates these assumptions, if exact-arithmetic equivalence is broken by numerical or implementation divergence, or if the validated regime (a 3B model, 32 sessions, 8K-token histories) does not match the reader's production scale or model family.

Median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average 68.98x across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, with approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding and a 3.42x reduction in additional session storage versus retained-boundary replay.
